title: Unipotent centre after removing the central multiplicative part
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. A group is of multiplicative type if over an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] it admits a closed subgroup inclusion into $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some $r\geq0$ [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type, def-sc-gm-ga]. Unipotent means admitting a closed group immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into some $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$, $n\geq1$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], where $\mathcal U_{n,k}(A)$ consists of upper triangular matrices with diagonal entries $1$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. The centre $Z(G)$ is the closed commutative subgroup of [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change]: its $A$-points commute with all $G(A^{\prime})$ after every commutative $A$-algebra extension $A^{\prime}$. Nilpotent means admitting a finite series $G=G_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq G_s=1$ of closed normal subgroup schemes with $[G(A),G_i(A)]\subseteq G_{i+1}(A)$ for all commutative $k$-algebras $A$ and all $i<s$. A represented fppf quotient has the meaning of [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]: the represented sheaf is the sheafification of $A\mapsto G(A)/N(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. Assume $G$ is connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] and nilpotent. Let $D\subseteq Z(G)$ be of multiplicative type and contain every subgroup of $Z(G)$ of multiplicative type. Let $q:G\to H$ represent $G/D$. Then $H$ is connected and nilpotent, and its scheme-theoretic centre $Z(H)$ is unipotent. No smoothness or perfectness is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 16.45 and its proof using Lemma 16.43, printed p.340. Connectedness of the quotient is Proposition 5.59, p.114; nilpotence descends by the images of a central series, Section 6.f. The lemma concludes unipotence of the centre, not of H.

proof.text: By affine normal-quotient geometry, $q$ has kernel $D$ and is faithfully flat, finitely presented and surjective. Thus $H$ is connected: a decomposition into disjoint clopen subsets pulls back to such a decomposition of $G$; connectedness of $G$ makes one pullback empty and surjectivity makes that subset empty. The identity of $H$ ensures nonemptiness.

source.place: Proposition 5.59(b), printed p.114; quotient geometry from Theorem 5.28, p.105.

proof.text: Choose the central series $G_i$ in the hypothesis. Factor each $G_i\to H$ as a faithfully flat homomorphism $u_i:G_i\to H_i$ followed by a closed group immersion, using affine homomorphism images. These give $H_0=H$, $H_s=1$ and $H_{i+1}\subseteq H_i$. Here and below closed-subgroup membership descends along faithfully flat algebra maps: if $J$ is the defining ideal and its values vanish after $A\to B$, they already vanish in $A$, by universal injectivity with module $A$. For $h\in H(A)$ and $y\in H_i(A)$, base change of $q$ along $h$ gives a faithfully flat algebra over which $h$ lifts to $g\in G$; a further base change of $u_i$ along $y$ lifts $y$ to $x\in G_i$. Over that algebra, $hyh^{-1}=q(gxg^{-1})$ belongs to $H_i$ and $[h,y]=q([g,x])$ belongs to $H_{i+1}$. Descend membership through the two injective algebra maps. This proves normality of $H_i$ and $[H(A),H_i(A)]\subseteq H_{i+1}(A)$ for every $A$. The same ideal test proves nesting from $G_{i+1}\subseteq G_i$, and the endpoints from $q$ and $G_s=1$. Hence the finite series $H_i$ proves nilpotence of $H$.

source.place: Definition 6.34 and Remark 6.35, printed p.133: descend the given central series through the quotient; Theorem 3.34, p.75, supplies closed faithfully flat images.

proof.text: The centre $C=Z(H)$ is a closed commutative affine subgroup. Apply the commutative multiplicative-part theorem to $C$ to obtain its largest multiplicative-type subgroup $S=C_s$, with $C/S$ unipotent. Since $S\subseteq Z(H)$ it is normal in $H$. Set $P=q^{-1}(S)$. Affine normal-quotient geometry gives a closed normal subgroup $P\subseteq G$ containing $D$, together with an exact sequence $1\to D\to P\to S\to1$ and the represented quotient $P/D\simeq S$.

source.place: Lemma 16.45, printed p.340, construction of the inverse image; Theorem 16.13(a), p.328, and Theorem 5.55, pp.112--113.

proof.text: Apply the normal multiplicative-layers lemma to the ambient connected group $G$ and its normal subgroups $D\subseteq P$. Its two multiplicative-type hypotheses hold: $D$ is so by assumption, and $P/D\simeq S$ is so by step 3. It follows that $P\subseteq Z(G)$ and $P$ is of multiplicative type. Maximality of $D$ inside $Z(G)$ gives $P\subseteq D$; together with $D\subseteq P$ this gives $P=D$. Therefore $S\simeq P/D=1$.

source.place: Lemma 16.45, printed p.340, application of Lemma 16.43 and maximality of the central multiplicative part.

proof.text: By step 3, $C/S$ is unipotent. Step 4 gives $S=1$, and the quotient of $C$ by the trivial subgroup is $C$ itself: $C(A)/1=C(A)$ on every algebra and the represented sheaf is already a sheaf. Thus the unitriangular closed immersion for $C/S$ gives one for $C=Z(H)$. This proves the remaining assertion without any smoothness or perfectness hypothesis.

source.place: Lemma 16.45, printed p.340, last inference via Theorem 16.13(a), p.328.
